title: SIU clears Toronto police in 2015 death of Rodrigo Almonacid Gonzalez
article: The province's Special Investigations Unit has cleared Toronto police in the 2015 death of 43-year-old Rodrigo Almonacid Gonzalez.
The SIU said police responded to a "panicked and frantic 911 call" at an apartment building at 10 Dora Ave., near Bloor Street and Lansdowne Avenue, just after midnight Nov. 6, 2015.
The first officer entered the unlocked apartment unit and found Gonzalez standing inside the bathroom holding a porcelain toilet lid above his head.
The officer demanded that Gonzalez drop the lid, and when he didn't, the officer slowly backed away.
A witness told officers that Gonzalez had gone on a rampage and that he had consumed cocaine.
"Because the officers were dealing with a barricaded individual, the Emergency Task Force was dispatched to assist," the SIU said in a news release Thursday, March 23.
When negotiations with Gonzalez failed, the ETF drilled a hole in the bathroom door in order to see him.

"They could see him sitting on the edge of the bathtub with blood on his hands, face and head, but he did not appear to be actively bleeding," the SIU said. "There was a stench of chemical cleaners, which caused the officers to become concerned that he had ingested noxious substances."
The door was then forced open, and the ETF officers entered the bathroom.
Gonzalez began lashing out, punching the officers. One officer deployed his Taser five times while another deployed the device three times before they gained control.
Gonzalez was taken to hospital with injuries that weren't considered serious at the time. He died in hospital the next day.
The cause of death was determined to be "complications of acute cocaine toxicity."
The SIU said the autopsy report didn't indicate that the Taser discharges played a role in the death.

"The circumstances surrounding the CEW (conducted energy weapon) discharge initially caused me great concern. I was particularly focused on the multiple and overlapping discharges applied to an individual who was wet and in a pool of water at the time," SIU director Tony Loparco said in the news release.
But Loparco said that he has no evidence of excessive use of force and that the CEW discharges by both subject officers were initially done at the behest of another officer.

"While it is worrisome that there were eight separate discharges by two different CEWs, some of which overlapped with one another, the evidence establishes that Mr. Almonacid Gonzalez was able to struggle through the pain and continue to resist the officers," Loparco said in the release. "Ultimately, there exists no evidentiary basis that allows me to attribute either the injuries or the death of Mr. Almonacid Gonzalez to the use of excessive force by the police."

The investigation included interviews with 13 civilian witnesses and 12 witness officers along with a review of a 12-minute audio recording that captured the negotiation, forced entry and Gonzalez's apprehension.
Neither subject officer took part in an SIU interview nor did they provide the agency with copies of their duty notes, as is their legal right.
